web_evidence.note: The complete text opens Part One with Harrison narrating as “I,” shifts to sustained external “he” narration in Part Two, returns to Harrison’s “we” and “I” in Part Three, and likewise contains a third-person backstory followed by Harrison’s first-person Part Five.

web_evidence.title: Novel to Film: An Introduction to the Theory of Adaptation
web_evidence.note: Brian McFarlane’s Clarendon Press structural analysis explicitly identifies Parts One, Three, and Five as narrated by Harrison and Parts Two and Four as third-person narration, including the novel’s movement between the two persons.

web_evidence.title: Best Adapted Screenplay: 1942
web_evidence.note: A review comparing novel and film independently describes the novel’s first-person Harrison narration and its subsequent movement into third person for Charles Rainier’s story.

person_note: The novel deliberately alternates sustained narrative persons: Harrison, a participating character, narrates Parts One, Three, and Five in the first person, while Parts Two and Four recount Rainier’s past in sustained third person. The supplied event excerpts chiefly come from the third-person backstory, whereas the dialogue excerpts do not identify narration; their lack of first-person evidence therefore does not contradict the full-book structure. The complete text and scholarly whole-book analysis independently agree, leaving only minor uncertainty about the local provenance of isolated q00509, not about the alternating classification.
